# Kamlesh Pattni

Ara Eve Leo Sal

1x

Kamlesh Mansukhlal Damji Pattni (born 1965) is a British-Kenyan businessman of Indian descent primarily known for masterminding the [Goldenberg scandal](/page/Goldenberg_scandal) in the 1990s, a scheme through his companies Goldenberg International Limited and Exchange Bank Limited that defrauded the Kenyan [government](/page/Government) of between US$600 million and US$1.5 billion via fictitious [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) [export](/page/Export) compensation claims, with minimal actual exports occurring.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1)[](#ref-2)[\[2\]](#ref-2) Born in [Mombasa](/page/Mombasa) to a [family](/page/Family) of [gold](/page/Gold) dealers, Pattni entered the trade early, securing [export](/page/Export) deals by age 25 and building a jewelry [business](/page/Business) before leveraging [government](/page/Government) incentives for the fraudulent operation, which implicated senior officials and contributed to Kenya's economic turmoil without resulting in any convictions despite judicial inquiries.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) Pattni's activities extended beyond Kenya, involving alleged bribery of Zimbabwean officials for illicit profits from [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) exports, exploitation of state assets, and ties to former President [Robert Mugabe](/page/Robert_Mugabe), as part of a broader network accused of [smuggling](/page/Smuggling) African [gold](/page/Gold) to fund [corruption](/page/Corruption) and evade sanctions.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) In [December](/page/December) 2024, the [United States](/page/United_States) designated him under [Executive Order](/page/Executive_order) 13818 for serious [human rights](/page/Human_rights) abuses and [corruption](/page/Corruption), including [money laundering](/page/Money_laundering) and resource misappropriation, while the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom) imposed parallel asset freezes, citing decades of [smuggling](/page/Smuggling) linked to child labor and even financing Russia's war in [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine); Pattni has denied these charges, including those from an Al Jazeera investigation into a "[gold](/page/Gold) [mafia](/page/Mafia)."[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3)[](#ref-2)[\[2\]](#ref-2) Despite the scandals, Pattni pursued ventures like a 2025 joint deal with Niger's [military government](/page/Military_government) to build a gold refinery and jewelry facility in [Niamey](/page/Niamey), positioning himself in West African resource extraction amid ongoing international scrutiny.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) He has also ventured into Kenyan [politics](/page/Politics), contesting a [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi) constituency seat with promises of development, though his reputation remains dominated by graft allegations rather than sustained legitimate enterprise.[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5)

## Early Life and Background

### Family Origins and Upbringing

Kamlesh Pattni was born in 1965 in [Mombasa](/page/Mombasa), [Kenya](/page/Kenya), specifically in the Kibokoni area near the historic Old Town and [Fort Jesus](/page/Fort_Jesus).[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5)[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) He grew up in a family engaged in the gold trade, with jewellery dealing forming a core part of their business activities.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4)[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6) Pattni has described his family's involvement in gold as a hereditary pursuit, stating in a 2025 interview that "it is in his blood" due to their longstanding jeweller background.[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6) His early years were marked by humble circumstances in Mombasa's coastal community, where he was exposed to the family's trade from a young age.[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5) As a young man, Pattni relocated to [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi), where he partnered with his brother to manage and expand a [jewellery](/page/Jewellery) enterprise, building on the familial foundation in precious metals.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) This move laid the groundwork for his entry into broader commercial ventures centered on [gold](/page/Gold) export and related dealings.[](#ref-7)[\[7\]](#ref-7)

### Education and Early Influences

Kamlesh Pattni was born on March 10, 1965, in [Mombasa](/page/Mombasa), [Kenya](/page/Kenya), to Mansukhlal Damji Pattni and his wife, a family of Indian descent originating from [Gujarat](/page/Gujarat).[](#ref-8)[\[8\]](#ref-8) Growing up in the coastal city's Kibokoni area near the Old Town, Pattni's early environment was shaped by the commercial vibrancy of Mombasa's trading communities, including Asian merchant families involved in local businesses such as textiles and imports, though his family's circumstances were described as modestly humble without inherited wealth.[](#ref-8)[\[8\]](#ref-8) [](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5) Pattni attended Allidina Visram High School, a prominent institution in [Mombasa](/page/Mombasa) serving the Asian community, where he completed his [secondary education](/page/Secondary_education).[](#ref-9)[\[9\]](#ref-9) He subsequently pursued higher education abroad, enrolling in a [Bachelor of Commerce](/page/Bachelor_of_Commerce) degree program at the [University of Münster](/page/University_of_Münster) in [Germany](/page/Germany), reflecting an early orientation toward [business studies](/page/Business_studies) amid Kenya's post-independence [economic liberalization](/page/Economic_liberalization).[](#ref-9)[\[9\]](#ref-9) This academic path likely influenced his subsequent entrepreneurial pursuits, emphasizing commercial acumen in [international trade](/page/International_trade) and [finance](/page/Finance), though specific mentors or pivotal early experiences beyond family mercantile exposure remain undocumented in available records.

## Business Career

### Initial Ventures and Rise

Pattni, born into a [Mombasa](/page/Mombasa) family of gold dealers from a [clan](/page/Clan) traditionally associated with goldsmithing, entered [business](/page/Business) through the jewelry [trade](/page/Trade). He co-operated Manorama Limited, a modest enterprise dealing in jewelry, alongside his brother on Dubois Road in [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi).[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) This venture reflected his inherited expertise in gold handling, which he described as a generational [trade](/page/Trade) "in our blood."[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6) After assuming family responsibilities following his father's death in an accident, which interrupted his studies in [Germany](/page/Germany), Pattni expanded into larger enterprises. In 1989, at age 24, he connected with influential figures like James Kanyotu, Kenya's [Special Branch](/page/Special_Branch) head, initially discussing [gold](/page/Gold)\-related opportunities.[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6) By July 11, 1990, he registered Goldenberg International Limited with KSh 100,000 in capital, positioning it for [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) exports amid Kenya's push for [foreign exchange](/page/The_Foreign_Exchange).[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) Kanyotu took a 25% stake in the company, lending operational leverage.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) Pattni's rise accelerated with the government's Export Compensation Scheme, launched on June 7, 1990, offering incentives for non-traditional exports. He secured Treasury approval from Finance Minister [George Saitoti](/page/George_Saitoti), committing Goldenberg to generate $50 million in foreign currency through exports.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) In August 1991, he founded Exchange Bank Limited with KSh 40 million capital, which became operational on June 4, 1992, to support these activities before its closure by the [Central Bank](/page/Central_bank) in 1993.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10)[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) By 1992, at age 27, Pattni had become an advisor to President [Daniel arap Moi](/page/Daniel_arap_Moi), elevating his profile in Kenyan business and political circles.[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6)

### Pre-Goldenberg Enterprises

Prior to establishing Goldenberg International Limited in [1990](/page/1990), Kamlesh Pattni's business endeavors were centered on the jewelry trade, building on his family's longstanding involvement in gold dealing in [Mombasa](/page/Mombasa).[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) Born in 1965 into this family of jewelers of Indian origin who had resided in [Kenya](/page/Kenya) for generations, Pattni entered the sector at a young age.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) Around [1990](/page/1990), at age 25, he relocated from [Mombasa](/page/Mombasa) to [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi) and partnered with his brother to manage Manorama Limited, a small-scale jewelry outlet situated on Dubois Road.[](#ref-11)[\[11\]](#ref-11) [](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) Manorama Limited focused on retailing [gold](/page/Gold) and silver ornaments, operating as a modest enterprise typical of family-influenced trading businesses in urban [Kenya](/page/Kenya) at the time.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) [](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) This venture represented Pattni's initial foray into independent operations beyond his coastal roots, though specific financial details or founding dates for Manorama remain undocumented in available records.[](#ref-11)[\[11\]](#ref-11) The business's location on Dubois Road positioned it within Nairobi's commercial hubs, facilitating local sales prior to Pattni's subsequent shift to larger premises on Moi Avenue's Mageso Chambers.[](#ref-11)[\[11\]](#ref-11) No evidence indicates involvement in export schemes, banking, or diversified enterprises during this period; Manorama appears to have been Pattni's sole documented pre-Goldenberg entity, reflecting a conventional entry into the gem and precious metals retail market.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) [](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) This phase underscores a transition from familial [gold](/page/Gold) dealing to urban retail, setting the stage for expanded ambitions in the early [1990s](/page/1990s).[](#ref-11)[\[11\]](#ref-11)

### Involvement in Export Schemes

Kamlesh Pattni, drawing from his family's background in gold dealing in Mombasa, initially operated Manorama Limited, a modest jewelry [business](/page/Business) on Nairobi's Dubois [Road](/page/Road) run alongside his brother.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) This venture laid the groundwork for his expansion into precious metals trade, but his significant involvement in export activities began with the Kenyan government's push to incentivize non-traditional exports.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) In response to Finance Minister George Saitoti's budget speech on June 7, 1990, which outlined enhanced export compensation to boost foreign exchange earnings, Pattni registered Goldenberg International Limited on July 11, 1990, with an initial capital of KSh 100,000.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) The company was positioned to engage in [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) exports, promising to generate $50 million in foreign exchange for [Kenya](/page/Kenya) through these activities.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) Under the Export Compensation Act—originally enacted in 1974 but expanded in the early 1990s—exporters could claim refunds on duties and a [percentage](/page/Percentage) incentive on verified export values, initially set at 20% but negotiated higher for strategic commodities like [gold](/page/Gold) and diamonds, reaching 35% in Pattni's case.[](#ref-12)[\[12\]](#ref-12)[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) Pattni's early participation involved submitting the first nine [export](/page/Export) compensation forms to First American Bank of [Kenya](/page/Kenya), using cash deposits to back claims of export proceeds.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10) These submissions aligned with the government's [policy](/page/Policy) to subsidize exports amid foreign [aid](/page/Aid) constraints, granting Goldenberg monopoly-like privileges on [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) dealings despite [Kenya](/page/Kenya)'s limited domestic production of these minerals.[](#ref-13)[\[13\]](#ref-13) By leveraging these incentives, Pattni's operations rapidly scaled, with Goldenberg receiving initial compensations that exceeded standard rates, setting the stage for deeper integration with state mechanisms for foreign exchange pre-financing.[](#ref-10)[\[10\]](#ref-10)[](#ref-12)[\[12\]](#ref-12)

## The Goldenberg Scandal

### Origins and Mechanics of the Scheme

The Goldenberg scheme originated in July 1990 when Kamlesh Pattni, a Kenyan businessman of Indian descent, and intelligence operative James Kanyotu incorporated Goldenberg International Limited to exploit Kenya's export incentive policies amid the country's economic challenges under President Daniel arap Moi's regime.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) Pattni, then in his mid-20s, positioned the company to handle [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) exports despite Kenya's negligible domestic production of these minerals, applying for special privileges including monopoly rights over such re-exports from third countries.[](#ref-14)[\[14\]](#ref-14) The scheme gained traction in 1991-1992 as Pattni lobbied Finance Minister [George Saitoti](/page/George_Saitoti) for enhanced subsidies, capitalizing on the government's desperation for [foreign exchange](/page/The_Foreign_Exchange) to fund political activities and counter multi-party reform pressures.[](#ref-15)[\[15\]](#ref-15) Mechanically, the fraud hinged on abusing the Export Compensation Act of 1974, which provided a 20% rebate on the value of non-traditional exports to encourage foreign currency inflows, with Pattni securing an additional 15% discretionary incentive from Saitoti, totaling 35%—far exceeding standard rates and not legally applicable to gold or diamonds.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) Goldenberg submitted falsified export documents claiming massive shipments of gold and diamonds—often re-exports of smuggled or imported goods from neighboring countries—to the Central Bank of Kenya, which disbursed subsidies in Kenyan shillings convertible to foreign exchange via Pattni's affiliated Exchange Bank Limited.[](#ref-15)[\[15\]](#ref-15) This process involved pre-shipment financing guarantees and cheque kiting to inflate transaction volumes, generating fictitious earnings on paper that rivaled Kenya's legitimate top exports like tea, while delivering no actual economic benefit as the claimed commodities were either non-existent or looped back without value addition.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) Pattni's operations funneled the subsidies—initially 5.8 billion Kenyan shillings (about $80 million at the time)—through Exchange Bank to offshore accounts and political slush funds, with complicit officials approving payments despite evident discrepancies in Kenya's mineral output records.[](#ref-15)[\[15\]](#ref-15) The scheme's scale escalated rapidly from 1991 to 1993, exploiting lax oversight in a [one-party state](/page/One-party_state), until an [International Monetary Fund](/page/International_Monetary_Fund) and World Bank audit in April 1993 exposed the irregularities, prompting the abolition of export subsidies in August 1993.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) While Pattni maintained the exports were legitimate re-exports, judicial inquiries later deemed the transactions fraudulent, attributing the mechanics to coordinated falsification rather than genuine trade.[](#ref-14)[\[14\]](#ref-14)

### Scale of Financial Impact

The Judicial Commission of Inquiry into the Goldenberg Affair, reporting in 2005, quantified the total financial transactions in the scandal at KSh 158.3 billion, encompassing fraudulent export compensation claims, pre-export financing, [foreign exchange](/page/The_Foreign_Exchange) manipulations, and payments to Goldenberg International Ltd (GIL) and 487 associated companies and individuals.[](#ref-16)[\[16\]](#ref-16)[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) This sum represented direct subsidies and illicit disbursements from the Kenyan Treasury and [Central Bank of Kenya](/page/Central_Bank_of_Kenya) (CBK) between 1990 and 1993, far exceeding legitimate [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) export values, which Kenya produced in negligible quantities.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1)[](#ref-17)[\[17\]](#ref-17) Direct payments to GIL alone totaled KSh 35,522,354,287.90, including KSh 5.8 billion in [export](/page/Export) compensation authorized via three Treasury letters dated April 19, June 28, and July 8, 1993, despite the scheme's termination in February 1993.[](#ref-16)[\[16\]](#ref-16) Additional components included KSh 13.5 billion in CBK foreign exchange allocations to Exchange Bank Ltd (EBL, controlled by Pattni) for fictitious inflows, KSh 8.36 billion in pre-[export](/page/Export) finance, and approximately KSh 10 billion in [cheque](/page/Cheque) kiting operations that inflated daily banking [liquidity](/page/Liquidity).[](#ref-16)[\[16\]](#ref-16) Losses from undelivered contracts, unrepaid credits, and interest shortfalls added at least KSh 27 billion in minimum quantifiable outlays.[](#ref-16)[\[16\]](#ref-16) Equivalent to about 10% of Kenya's GDP in the early 1990s, the scandal's scale triggered macroeconomic instability, including shilling devaluation from KSh 9.25 to KSh 16.29 per USD between August and December 1992, [inflation](/page/Inflation) surging from 11.6% to 18.6% over 1990-1991, and widened budget deficits necessitating higher domestic borrowing.[](#ref-16)[\[16\]](#ref-16)[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) It contributed to a [balance-of-payments crisis](/page/Crisis), prompting IMF suspension of [aid](/page/Aid) in 1997 amid governance concerns over the affair's exposure.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1)[](#ref-12)[\[12\]](#ref-12) Funds were often transferred abroad without repatriation, with KSh 6.09 billion in purported [foreign exchange](/page/The_Foreign_Exchange) proceeds unaccounted for.[](#ref-16)[\[16\]](#ref-16)

### Investigations, Trials, and Legal Outcomes

The Goldenberg scandal triggered multiple investigations beginning in the mid-1990s, following whistleblower revelations and audits by the Central Bank of Kenya that exposed irregularities in export compensation claims by Goldenberg International Ltd., owned by Pattni.[](#ref-18)[\[18\]](#ref-18) A pivotal probe was the Judicial Commission of Inquiry into the Goldenberg Affair, appointed in February 2003 by President Mwai Kibaki and chaired by Justice Abdul Majid Cockar, which examined over 1,000 documents and heard testimony from Pattni and associates.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) The commission's 2005 report detailed fraudulent claims totaling KSh 158.3 billion (approximately US$2.3 billion at 2003 exchange rates), attributing the scheme's orchestration to Pattni through fictitious exports and undue compensations exceeding 20% of claim values, and recommended criminal prosecution of Pattni alongside officials like former Finance Minister Arthur Magugu and Central Bank Governor Elkanah Sambili.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) [](#ref-19)[\[19\]](#ref-19) Subsequent probes by the Kenya Anti-Corruption Commission (KACC, predecessor to EACC) from 2003 onward focused on Pattni, filing suits against him and 16 co-accused in October 2003 under [anti-corruption](/page/Anti-corruption) laws for conspiracy, abuse of office, and [money laundering](/page/Money_laundering) tied to Sh5.8 billion in illicit payments.[](#ref-20)[\[20\]](#ref-20) Pattni's first [arrest](/page/Arrest) occurred in March 1994 on related [fraud](/page/Fraud) suspicions, followed by 1998 charges for [forging](/page/Forging) signatures on compensation documents, which he contested via [High Court](/page/High_court) prohibition orders in 1997 and 2001, halting proceedings on jurisdictional grounds.[](#ref-18)[\[18\]](#ref-18) [](#ref-21)[\[21\]](#ref-21) Revived under the 2003 [anti-corruption](/page/Anti-corruption) framework, prosecutions intensified in 2008 with 40 counts against Pattni for defrauding the state through exaggerated diamond and gold export claims, involving witnesses from the [Central Bank](/page/Central_bank) and [Treasury](/page/Treasury).[](#ref-22)[\[22\]](#ref-22) Pattni's trials spanned over two decades, marked by delays, witness recantations, and appeals; he maintained innocence, arguing legitimate business under government policy and prosecutorial overreach.[](#ref-23)[\[23\]](#ref-23) In 2013, [High Court](/page/High_court) Justice Joseph Mutava acquitted Pattni of all charges, ruling the prolonged process constituted abuse of court process and violating fair trial rights under the [constitution](/page/Constitution), while barring further pursuit on the same facts.[](#ref-22)[\[22\]](#ref-22) Remaining civil and criminal matters culminated in 2020 rulings: on July 3, the [High Court](/page/High_court) quashed all charges, citing evidential deficiencies and prior determinations; on December 24, Milimani Magistrate's Court formally terminated proceedings, absolving Pattni and his firms.[](#ref-24)[\[24\]](#ref-24) [](#ref-25)[\[25\]](#ref-25) No convictions resulted from Goldenberg prosecutions, including Pattni's, despite commission recommendations, with outcomes attributed to procedural flaws rather than exoneration of underlying conduct.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1) [](#ref-26)[\[26\]](#ref-26)

### Pattni's Defense and Broader Implications

Pattni has maintained that the Goldenberg scheme operated legitimately under the Export Compensation Act of 1990, which incentivized non-traditional exports including gold and diamonds, and that it injected vital foreign exchange into Kenya's economy during the 1989–1994 crisis by facilitating remittances and trade. He attributes the scandal's negative framing to business rivals, entrenched cartels, and a [Central Bank of Kenya](/page/Central_Bank_of_Kenya) (CBK) whistleblower, while denying personal responsibility and insisting he neither controlled government policy nor the CBK's payment approvals. In a June 2025 interview, Pattni expressed no regrets over the affair, rejecting [repentance](/page/Repentance) as unwarranted and portraying his role as economically beneficial and divinely inspired, while accusing the CBK of exploiting the [scandal](/page/Scandal) to obscure its own extensions of unsecured loans to politically connected entities.[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6)[](#ref-27)[\[27\]](#ref-27) Legally, Pattni's defense centered on violations of his constitutional [rights](/page/Rights) to a fair and [speedy trial](/page/Speedy_trial), citing over two decades of prosecutorial delays, lost documents, deceased or unavailable witnesses, prejudicial media coverage undermining his [presumption of innocence](/page/Presumption_of_innocence), and prior settlements that negated ongoing claims. [High Court](/page/High_court) Justice Joseph Mutava acquitted him in March 2013, ruling under Article 50 of the Kenyan Constitution that further proceedings would be abusive, given the CBK's withdrawal as complainant after Pattni surrendered the Grand Regency Hotel (valued at billions of shillings) and Treasury bills, alongside a Sh2.4 billion restitution in a [plea bargain](/page/Plea_bargain) with the Kenya Anti-Corruption Commission. Remaining charges were quashed in [July](/page/July) 2020, formally terminating the criminal case.[](#ref-24)[\[24\]](#ref-24)[](#ref-25)[\[25\]](#ref-25) The acquittal drew scrutiny, as Mutava was later dismissed in 2019 by the Judicial Service Commission for gross misconduct, including irregularly retrieving the case from [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi) to [Kericho](/page/Kericho) for adjudication, which critics viewed as procedural irregularity favoring Pattni. Despite this, no appeals overturned the ruling, reflecting evidentiary challenges in prosecuting complex, decades-old financial [fraud](/page/Fraud) amid political transitions from the Moi era. Pattni has also denied broader criminality tied to Goldenberg, emphasizing legal compliance in [export](/page/Export) claims processed through state mechanisms.[](#ref-28)[\[28\]](#ref-28)[](#ref-29)[\[29\]](#ref-29)[](#ref-26)[\[26\]](#ref-26) The [Goldenberg scandal](/page/Goldenberg_scandal) imposed direct losses estimated at $600 million to $1.5 billion—equivalent to up to 10% of Kenya's [1990s](/page/1990s) GDP—through fictitious export claims yielding no verifiable [gold](/page/Gold) or [diamond](/page/Diamond) outflows, draining foreign reserves and necessitating IMF bailouts amid [hyperinflation](/page/Hyperinflation) and debt crises. It exemplified causal failures in policy design, where the 20% compensation rate on export values, combined with lax verification in a [one-party state](/page/One-party_state), enabled private capture of public funds via approvals from the [presidency](/page/Presidency), [treasury](/page/Treasury), and CBK, fostering a [patronage](/page/Patronage) system that prioritized elite interests over fiscal prudence.[](#ref-1)[\[1\]](#ref-1)[](#ref-30)[\[30\]](#ref-30) Institutionally, the [affair](/page/Affair) eroded trust in core bodies like the CBK, [judiciary](/page/Judiciary), and attorney general's office, as the [2003](/page/2003) Bosire Commission documented systemic complicity yet yielded no high-level convictions due to witness [intimidation](/page/Intimidation), evidentiary gaps, and prosecutorial [inertia](/page/Inertia) under successive regimes. This [impunity](/page/Impunity) normalized grand [corruption](/page/Corruption), influencing subsequent scandals and hindering economic reforms by deterring foreign investment and perpetuating elite [impunity](/page/Impunity), with Pattni's persistence in gold trade underscoring unresolved vulnerabilities in resource governance across [East Africa](/page/East_Africa).[](#ref-16)[\[16\]](#ref-16)[](#ref-31)[\[31\]](#ref-31)

## Political Involvement

### Entry into Politics

Kamlesh Pattni entered Kenyan politics in late 2006 by assuming the chairmanship of the Kenya [National Democratic Alliance](/page/National_Democratic_Alliance) (KENDA), a minor [party](/page/Party) originally founded in 1992 by academic David Mukaru Ng’ang’a.[](#ref-32)[\[32\]](#ref-32) He was recruited by party officials Joram Kariuki and Pius Njogu, who persuaded him to revitalize the organization ahead of the 2007 general elections; under his leadership, KENDA adopted a new party symbol of a bell and the slogan "Awakening."[](#ref-32)[\[32\]](#ref-32) Pattni positioned himself as the party's candidate for the Westlands parliamentary constituency in [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi), framing his involvement as an application of business acumen to public governance for poverty reduction, guided by what he described as [divine inspiration](/page/Divine_inspiration) rather than personal ambition.[](#ref-32)[\[32\]](#ref-32)[](#ref-33)[\[33\]](#ref-33) This marked his formal debut as a [politician](/page/_Politician_), despite earlier informal ties to ruling circles during the 1990s Goldenberg affair and a declined nomination offer from the [Kenya African National Union](/page/Kenya_African_National_Union) (KANU) in 1992, which he attributed to his youth and inexperience at the time.[](#ref-32)[\[32\]](#ref-32) KENDA fielded multiple candidates in the December 2007 elections, leveraging Pattni's financial resources to secure nominations, though the party achieved limited success overall.[](#ref-34)[\[34\]](#ref-34)

### Electoral Campaigns and Positions

In 2013, Pattni sought election as [Member of Parliament](/page/Member_of_parliament) for the [Westlands constituency](/page/Westlands_Constituency) in [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi) under the Kenya National Democratic Alliance (KENDA).[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5) His campaign emphasized a humanitarian approach, rejecting [tribalism](/page/Tribalism) in favor of equality and positioning [Kenya](/page/Kenya) as "God's own country" through development initiatives.[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5) Pattni pledged to eradicate slums by providing modern housing, create employment opportunities, alleviate poverty, and establish a Religious Development Fund to support faith-based community projects.[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5) Despite his central role in the [Goldenberg scandal](/page/Goldenberg_scandal), which had defrauded [Kenya](/page/Kenya) of billions of shillings, Pattni campaigned as "Brother Paul," leveraging his conversion to evangelical [Christianity](/page/Christianity) and leadership at Hope International Church to appeal to voters in impoverished areas, where supporters distributed food, flour, and cash.[](#ref-35)[\[35\]](#ref-35) He lost the election on March 4, 2013.[](#ref-35)[\[35\]](#ref-35) Pattni's political positions centered on economic upliftment tied to religious values, advocating for policies that prioritized the "downtrodden" through direct aid and infrastructure improvements.[](#ref-35)[\[35\]](#ref-35) Earlier, in the 1990s, he had supported Kenya African National Union (KANU) campaigns financially, disbursing approximately 4.8 billion Kenyan shillings to politicians and influencers ahead of the 1992 multiparty elections, though this reflected patronage rather than personal candidacy.[](#ref-36)[\[36\]](#ref-36) His brief association with the Safina party ended acrimoniously in 1998, when he accused leader Paul Muite of extorting 20 million Kenyan shillings from him.[](#ref-37)[\[37\]](#ref-37) No successful electoral bids or appointed positions followed his 2013 defeat.

### Associations with Kenyan Governments

Pattni's business operations were closely intertwined with the administration of President [Daniel arap Moi](/page/Daniel_arap_Moi), who authorized export compensation schemes that disproportionately benefited Pattni's Goldenberg International Limited in the early 1990s. During parliamentary inquiries, Pattni testified that he personally delivered suitcases containing millions of Kenyan shillings in cash to Moi's office as commissions, though Moi denied receiving such payments.[](#ref-38)[\[38\]](#ref-38)[](#ref-39)[\[39\]](#ref-39) This relationship enabled Pattni to secure government contracts and licenses amid Kenya's foreign aid embargo, facilitating the export of purportedly Kenyan [gold](/page/Gold) that investigations later suggested included smuggled minerals from neighboring countries.[](#ref-40)[\[40\]](#ref-40) Under President Mwai Kibaki's government (2002–2013), Pattni faced intensified scrutiny through renewed Goldenberg investigations and indictments in 2006, yet he cultivated ongoing associations, as evidenced by photographs he displayed of meetings with Kibaki.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) In 2007, Pattni entered formal politics by assuming the chairmanship of the Kenya National Democratic Alliance (KENDA), positioning himself as a political figure amid Kibaki's tenure.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) Despite legal challenges, Pattni was acquitted of Goldenberg-related charges by [2013](/page/2013), after which he ran as a parliamentary candidate for the [Westlands constituency](/page/Westlands_Constituency) in [Nairobi](/page/Nairobi), leveraging perceived political protections to sustain his influence.[](#ref-35)[\[35\]](#ref-35) Pattni's interactions with the subsequent [Uhuru Kenyatta](/page/Uhuru_Kenyatta) administration (2013–2022) were primarily adversarial, centered on legal disputes such as his 2020 lawsuit against a [tribunal](/page/Tribunal) investigating [judicial misconduct](/page/Judicial_misconduct), which he claimed unfairly implicated him in unrelated probes.[](#ref-41)[\[41\]](#ref-41) No substantive business or advisory roles linking Pattni to Kenyatta's government have been documented, contrasting with his earlier ties to Moi and Kibaki.[](#ref-42)[\[42\]](#ref-42)

## International Business and Controversies

### Expansion into African Gold Trade

Following the [Goldenberg scandal](/page/Goldenberg_scandal) in [Kenya](/page/Kenya) during the [1990s](/page/1990s), which centered on fictitious [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) exports compensated through government subsidies, Kamlesh Pattni redirected his business interests toward actual [gold](/page/Gold) trading operations across other African countries, often involving [smuggling](/page/Smuggling) and [bribery](/page/Bribery) to exploit natural resources.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) His network established a presence in resource-rich nations, utilizing front companies and political connections to facilitate illicit exports and [money laundering](/page/Money_laundering), with activities documented as early as the [1990s](/page/1990s) in [southern Africa](/page/Southern_Africa).[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) In [Zimbabwe](/page/Zimbabwe), Pattni cultivated ties with high-level officials, including former President [Robert Mugabe](/page/Robert_Mugabe), to enable [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamond](/page/Diamond) [export](/page/Export) fraud, including overreporting cash proceeds to claim [export](/page/Export) incentives and laundering illicit funds through [gold](/page/Gold) purchases.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) Operating via entities such as Suzan General Trading (PVT) LTD and Skorus Investments (PVT) LTD, his scheme involved transporting undeclared U.S. dollars to [Harare](/page/Harare), converting them into [gold](/page/Gold), and exporting the refined product to [Dubai](/page/Dubai) for a 10% commission, thereby masking origins and evading taxes.[](#ref-23)[\[23\]](#ref-23) These operations, exposed in investigative reporting, relied on bribing Zimbabwean authorities for protection and preferential treatment in the gold trade.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3)[](#ref-23)[\[23\]](#ref-23) Pattni's expansion extended to [West Africa](/page/West_Africa), exemplified by a [joint venture](/page/Joint_venture) signed on April 23, 2025, with the Nigerien government under its [military junta](/page/Military_junta).[](#ref-43)[\[43\]](#ref-43) Through his Dubai-based firm Suvarna Royal Gold Trading LLC, the agreement formed Royal Gold Niger SA to construct Niger's first domestic [gold](/page/Gold) [refinery](/page/Refinery), a jewelry [manufacturing](/page/Manufacturing) [plant](/page/Plant), and a gemstone-cutting facility near [Niamey](/page/Niamey), aiming to process the country's $547 million in annual [gold](/page/Gold) exports locally.[](#ref-43)[\[43\]](#ref-43) [Niger](/page/Niger) retains an equity stake, though specific financial terms remain undisclosed; this deal proceeded despite Pattni's December 2024 sanctions by the U.S. and U.K. for global [gold](/page/Gold) smuggling.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3)[](#ref-43)[\[43\]](#ref-43) The venture positions Pattni to capture value in [Niger](/page/Niger)'s burgeoning [gold](/page/Gold) sector, competing with regional refineries in [Ghana](/page/Ghana) and [Burkina Faso](/page/Burkina_Faso).[](#ref-43)[\[43\]](#ref-43)

### Operations in Zimbabwe, DRC, and Niger

Kamlesh Pattni's operations in Zimbabwe centered on illicit gold and diamond smuggling, primarily through his company Suzan General Trading (PVT) LTD, which facilitated the export of undeclared minerals to Dubai for laundering.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) A 2023 Al Jazeera investigation, "Gold Mafia," revealed Pattni's network bribing Zimbabwean officials to secure export licenses and overreport cash inflows, depriving the state of revenues estimated in millions from gold sales.[](#ref-44)[\[44\]](#ref-44) Pattni, who claimed close ties to President Emmerson Mnangagwa, used intermediaries to purchase gold from artisanal miners and state entities like the Zimbabwe Gold Mafia, then laundered proceeds via UAE-based firms such as Sun Multinational DMCC.[](#ref-45)[\[45\]](#ref-45) These activities, exposed as systematic evasion of export duties, prompted U.S. and UK sanctions in December 2024 against Pattni and associates for facilitating corruption and money laundering.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) [](#ref-2)[\[2\]](#ref-2) Pattni denied involvement in smuggling, asserting his firms operated legally.[](#ref-2)[\[2\]](#ref-2) Evidence of direct operations in the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](/page/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo) (DRC) remains limited, with Pattni's network primarily documented in Zimbabwean smuggling rather than DRC-specific extraction or export schemes.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) Historical ties trace to the 1990s [Goldenberg scandal](/page/Goldenberg_scandal), where Pattni allegedly sourced non-existent gold exports attributed to DRC (then [Zaire](/page/Zaire)) to claim Kenyan subsidies, but recent activities focus southward.[](#ref-46)[\[46\]](#ref-46) Broader gold trade discussions in investigations mention DRC-sourced minerals entering regional networks, potentially overlapping with Pattni's Dubai refining, though no verified [bribery](/page/Bribery) or company deployments in the DRC are attributed to him.[](#ref-23)[\[23\]](#ref-23) In [Niger](/page/Niger), Pattni secured a [joint venture](/page/Joint_venture) in April 2025 with the [military junta](/page/Military_junta) government to construct the country's first gold refinery and jewelry complex near [Niamey](/page/Niamey), partnering through his Dubai-based Suvarna Royal Gold Trading LLC.[](#ref-4)[\[4\]](#ref-4) The deal, valued for processing local artisanal gold and reducing export losses, includes a gemstone polishing center and aims to refine up to domestic production levels, despite Pattni's prior sanctions for Zimbabwean illicit trade.[](#ref-47)[\[47\]](#ref-47) Critics, including U.S. alerts, flagged risks of exploiting post-coup instability for personal gain, echoing patterns in Pattni's [Zimbabwe](/page/Zimbabwe) ventures.[](#ref-14)[\[14\]](#ref-14) The Nigerien partnership proceeded amid international scrutiny, with Pattni positioning it as legitimate investment in under-refined African gold sectors.[](#ref-48)[\[48\]](#ref-48)

### Recent Sanctions and Allegations

In December 2024, the [United States](/page/United_States) Department of the Treasury's [Office of Foreign Assets Control](/page/Office_of_Foreign_Assets_Control) (OFAC) designated Kamlesh Pattni and 27 associated individuals and entities under the Global Magnitsky [Human Rights](/page/Human_rights) Accountability Act for their roles in a transnational gold smuggling and [money laundering](/page/Money_laundering) network centered in [Zimbabwe](/page/Zimbabwe).[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) The sanctions targeted Pattni as the leader of this network, which allegedly bribed Zimbabwean officials to facilitate illicit exports of [gold](/page/Gold) and [diamonds](/page/The_Diamonds), exploited export incentive fraud schemes, and laundered proceeds through couriers and shell companies in the [United Arab Emirates](/page/United_Arab_Emirates) and elsewhere.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) These measures froze assets under U.S. jurisdiction and prohibited American persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties, aiming to disrupt corruption enabling [human rights](/page/Human_rights) abuses and undermining [Zimbabwe](/page/Zimbabwe)'s economy.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) Concurrently, the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom) imposed sanctions on Pattni, his wife Minal Kamlesh Mansukhlal Damji Pattni, and brother-in-law Mukesh Vaya under its Global Anti-Corruption Sanctions regime, citing their involvement in bribery and [money laundering](/page/Money_laundering) linked to international [gold](/page/Gold) trading.[](#ref-2)[\[2\]](#ref-2) The UK's [National Crime Agency](/page/National_Crime_Agency) froze Pattni's UK-based assets, including properties, and imposed travel bans, with allegations extending to laundering Russian illicit funds via UAE-based entities.[](#ref-26)[\[26\]](#ref-26) Pattni's network was implicated in Al Jazeera's 2023 "Gold Mafia" documentary, which exposed [smuggling](/page/Smuggling) operations evading Zimbabwe's export controls and generating untaxed revenues estimated in millions of dollars annually.[](#ref-2)[\[2\]](#ref-2) Pattni has denied the money laundering accusations, asserting no involvement in illicit activities and framing the sanctions as politically motivated.[](#ref-2)[\[2\]](#ref-2) U.S. and [UK](/page/United_Kingdom) authorities, however, described the network's operations as systematically corrupt, with Pattni enlisting family and associates to move undeclared [gold](/page/Gold) via air couriers and falsified [documentation](/page/Documentation), profiting from undervalued exports and evading over $100 million in potential taxes and duties in [Zimbabwe](/page/Zimbabwe) alone.[](#ref-3)[\[3\]](#ref-3) No criminal charges have been filed against Pattni in these jurisdictions as of October 2025, but the designations bar him from accessing Western financial systems, complicating his business ventures in African [gold](/page/Gold) sectors.[](#ref-26)[\[26\]](#ref-26)

## Personal Life

### Family and Relationships

Kamlesh Pattni is married to Minal Kamlesh Mansuklall Damji Pattni, born February 25, 1975, in [Kenya](/page/Kenya), who holds a degree from the [University of Leicester](/page/University_of_Leicester).[](#ref-49)[\[49\]](#ref-49)[](#ref-50)[\[50\]](#ref-50) The couple has two children: a [daughter](/page/Daughter) named Ruhi and a son named Mir. In July 2020, Ruhi was four years old and Mir was two.[](#ref-49)[\[49\]](#ref-49) In December 2024, the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom) sanctioned both Pattni and his wife Minal under its Global Anti-Corruption Sanctions regime for their roles in an international network involving [bribery](/page/Bribery) of Zimbabwean officials and laundering of illicit gold and diamond proceeds through entities in the [United Arab Emirates](/page/United_Arab_Emirates).[](#ref-50)[\[50\]](#ref-50) Pattni's brother-in-law, Mukesh Vaya, was similarly sanctioned for facilitating [money laundering](/page/Money_laundering) tied to Russian funds via UAE-based companies linked to Pattni's operations.[](#ref-51)[\[51\]](#ref-51) No [public records](/page/Public_records) indicate prior marriages or additional [immediate family](/page/Immediate_family) members.

### Religious and Philanthropic Activities

Following his acquittal in the [Goldenberg scandal](/page/Goldenberg_scandal) prosecutions, Kamlesh Pattni converted to [Christianity](/page/Christianity) and adopted the name Brother Paul, reinventing himself as an evangelical pastor.[](#ref-26)[\[26\]](#ref-26)[](#ref-52)[\[52\]](#ref-52) He founded Hope International Ministry in [Kenya](/page/Kenya), an evangelistic organization modeled after the biblical Apostle Paul, focused on planting churches before transitioning to new locations.[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6) Through the ministry, Pattni has preached in multiple countries, including [Kenya](/page/Kenya), the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom), [Zimbabwe](/page/Zimbabwe), [Antigua and Barbuda](/page/Antigua_and_Barbuda), and collaborated with figures such as former [Mungiki](/page/Mungiki) sect leader Maina Njenga, whom he appointed to lead preaching efforts in [Kenya](/page/Kenya).[](#ref-6)[\[6\]](#ref-6) Pattni established the Hand of Hope Foundation (initially known as the Kamlesh Pattni Welfare Foundation) as a charitable [non-governmental organization](/page/Non-governmental_organization) to support humanitarian efforts, particularly aiding the poor, oppressed, and those denied justice.[](#ref-52)[\[52\]](#ref-52)[](#ref-8)[\[8\]](#ref-8) The foundation's activities include providing daily financial and material assistance, digging boreholes for [water](/page/Water) access, distributing [food](/page/Food), operating orphanages, funding [education](/page/Education) and medical treatments, offering free [legal aid](/page/Legal_aid), and running a nationwide program to supply sanitary towels to schoolgirls in rural and [slum](/page/Slum) areas to reduce [absenteeism](/page/Absenteeism).[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5)[](#ref-53)[\[53\]](#ref-53) Specific contributions by [Hand of Hope](/page/Hand_of_Hope) under Pattni's involvement encompass donating nine tractors to the Mijikenda community for agricultural support, supplying mattresses, grains, stationery, and a [vehicle](/page/Vehicle) to a church in Kerio [Valley](/page/Valley), contributing KSh 200,000 to St. Mary’s ACK Church for construction, sponsoring [surgery](/page/Surgery) for a boy with Hirschsprung disease, installing boreholes in Kajiado Central, and improving market infrastructure in Westlands.[](#ref-5)[\[5\]](#ref-5)[](#ref-49)[\[49\]](#ref-49) These initiatives align with Pattni's stated post-conversion focus on [philanthropy](/page/Philanthropy), though they have coincided with his broader political and business endeavors.[](#ref-8)[\[8\]](#ref-8)

An international gold smuggling and money laundering network exposed by Al Jazeera’s Investigative Unit (I-Unit) has been sanctioned by the US and UK governments. The measures, including asset freezes, confiscation of property and travel bans, target Kenyan-British businessman, Kamlesh Pattni.

Pattni allegedly bribed officials in Zimbabwe to earn illicit profits from the country’s gold and diamond trade. He is also accused of moving dirty money, using his global business empire that extends from Zimbabwe and Dubai to Singapore and London to launder it.

The US Department of Treasury said that Pattni’s fraudulent scheme “has robbed Zimbabwe’s citizens of the benefit of those natural resources while enriching corrupt government officials and criminal actors”.

“Across the globe, when corrupt actors like Pattni choose to exploit openings in governance structures to benefit themselves and their cronies, communities suffer and public trust is undermined,” Acting Undersecretary of the Treasury for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence Bradley T Smith said in [a statement released](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy2740) by the US Treasury Department.

## Goldenberg Scandal

Pattni was born in Kenya, where he became notorious in the 1990s for his alleged role in the so-called Goldenberg Scandal, a gold smuggling scheme that is believed to have robbed Kenya of $600m – equivalent to 10 percent of the country’s gross domestic product at the time and led to charges of corruption against many members of then-President Daniel Arap Moi’s government. After years of prosecution, Pattni was acquitted. He has since reinvented himself as an evangelical pastor, known as Brother Paul.

Advertisement

Pattni featured prominently in I-Unit’s [Gold Mafia](https://www.ajiunit.com/investigation/gold-mafia-smuggle-zimbabwe-rudland-macmillan-pattni/), broadcast in 2023. The four-part investigation revealed the criminal gangs that control gold exports in Southern Africa for the benefit of corrupt politicians and launder their profits around the world.

Undercover reporters from the I-Unit [met Pattni](/news/2023/3/23/gold-smuggler-pattni-kenya-zimbabwe) who was quick to boast of his political influence in Africa, showing reporters photos with several African leaders – from former Libyan President Muammar Gaddafi to ex-Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe.

Pattni described how his businesses in Zimbabwe relied on the political support from President Emmerson Mnangagwa and how an employee would pay regular bribes to the president to keep him on side. “When you work, you must always have the king with you, the president”, Pattni told the reporters.

Mnangagwa did not respond to the I-Unit’s requests for comment.

## Front companies

The I-Unit’s undercover reporters claimed to be Chinese gangsters with more than $100m of dirty cash they needed clean. Pattni described a way to launder the dirty money by using it to fund his gold-buying operations in Zimbabwe.

Pattni described how his companies could be used as a front for illicit activity and give the criminal operations a veneer of legitimacy. He told the reporters the gold would be flown to Dubai, where it would be imported by companies also owned by Pattni. Once those companies sold the gold, the proceeds would be banked and the money would be clean.

The undercover reporters were invited to Dubai by Pattni who took them on a tour of his companies and introduced them to key figures in his operation. Many of them are named among the 27 companies and individuals in Pattni’s network sanctioned by the US Treasury.

As well as undercover meetings with Pattni, the I-Unit’s investigators obtained a trove of files from inside Pattni’s operation and spoke to whistleblowers who explained the inner workings of his operation, including bribery at Zimbabwe’s national gold refinery and smuggling at Harare Airport.

When asked to explain the revelations emerging from Al Jazeera’s investigation, Pattni denied any criminal wrongdoing in Kenya and emphasised that he had never been convicted in relation to his activities in that country. He denied involvement in any kind of money laundering, as well as employing anyone to smuggle cash or offering to deal with funds he knew originated from illegal sources.

He said that when he met Al Jazeera’s undercover team, he thought he was meeting an investor who wanted to buy a stake in hotel businesses and “to divest of a portfolio in China into gold buying and mining in Zimbabwe”.

Besides this investigation, Gold Mafia [revealed](/news/2023/3/23/gold-mafia-godmen-conmen-president-niece) several other gold smuggling operations in Southern Africa.

Received 24 August 2017, Accepted 10 October 2017

ABSTRACT:

Corruption has become an issue of major political and economic relevance in recent years. This has led to a

resurgence of interest in analyzing the phenomenon and the diverse forms that it assumes in developing politics

with an expectation that democratization and economic liberation offer potential routes to dealing with the

problem. Anti-corruption strategies range from institutional reforms through concerted efforts at the international,

populist and local levels, but the efficiency of these approaches has not been subject to careful empirical research.

This study examines these issues with reference to the politics and practicalities of anti-corruption strategies in

several African societies. It is posited that although right sizing the state and political liberalization are desirable

goals in many African states, they are necessary rather than sufficient conditions for the reduction of corruption.

Extensive public and private sector corruption can coexist with democratic politics. Economic liberalization can

also create avenues for corruption, through the sale of parastatals in dubious circumstances. For anti-corruption

strategies to be effective in the continent, more attention needs to be devoted to questions of sequencing, the

details of reform and its sustainability in very poor polities, political will and commitment.

Keywords: African, Corruption, Anti graft agencies

INTRODUCTION

In recent years corruption has become an

issue of major econo-political significance in

many countries across the globe, including a

number of developed Western States. Corruption

scandals are a prominent source of media

interest and newspapers frequently publish

stories about illicit behaviors by politicians and

public officials. Partly on account of heightened

media attention there is widespread perception

that corruption is on the increase, both among

the general public who demand effective action

and politicians who are eager to derive political

capital by adopting a forthright stance over the

need to eliminate corrupt practices (Heywood,

1997 and Eme, et al, 2008). This has resulted in

the increased electoral popularity of political

parties committed to fighting corruption and the

launching of high profile anti-corruption

campaigns by governments of various

ideological hues. Specialized non-governmental

organizations (NGOs) have been established in a

number of countries to publicize the problem of

corruption and mobilize public concern around

cases of malfeasance as a means of provoking of

official response. At the international level there

is increased resolve on the part of inter-

governmental bodies such as the Organization

for Economic Cooperation and Development

(OECD) and the World Bank to tackle the

problem of corruption in response to rising

concern about aid effectiveness at a time of

financial stringency and to public criticism

(Robinson, 1998).

While corruption is a feature of all societies

to varying degrees, it is a particular concern for

developing polities because it undermines

economic growth, discourages foreign

investment and reduces the resources available

for infrastructure, public services and anti-

poverty programs (World Bank, 1997). As noted

by Johnston (1997), it may also undermine

political institutions by weakening the

legitimacy and accountability of governments.

Corruption also reduces the effectiveness of aid\-

funded development projects and weakens

public support for development assistance in

donor countries. In short, it is inimical to

sustainable development, poverty reduction and

good governance, though it can also have the

opposite effect by circumventing cumbersome

regulations and facilitating business transactions

(Ades and Di. Tella, 1996).

African effort in terms of mitigating

corruption at continental and even national level

has been very feeble and inconsistent at best. Till

date, there has not been any serious and

concerted effort inform of effective policy or

strategy towards addressing this awesome

problem. There are so many reasons for this. As

Odenkunle (1986) and World Bank (1997)

suggest, the problem with fighting corruption in

developing countries especially in Africa is that

everybody in government is deeply involved.

From the Head of State, Ministers, State and

Local council officers down to the lowest ranks

of public officer, the primary motivating factor

is basically how to use official position to gain

illicit advantage of whatever form to the overall

detriment of the state and the economic system.

Apart from Nigeria which recently launched

a frontal assault on corruption starting from the

leadership and the passage of an Anti-corruption

Acts and possibly, South Africa, Namibia,

Botswana, Uganda, Ghana, and Malawi, and

Kenya with their domestic anti-corruption

initiatives, most other sub-Saharan African states

have not done much either in terms of creating

genuine anti-corruption policy or program or to

embark upon institutional and administrative

reforms. As a result, practically nothing has been

done at the continental level to tackle this

problem.

This paper seeks to fill in this gap. This study

examines these issues with reference to the

politics and practicalities of anti-corruption

strategies in several African Societies. It is

argued that although institutional reforms are

desirable goals in many African countries, they

are necessary rather than sufficient conditions

for the reduction of corruption. The first section

of the paper clarifies and identifies forms and

typologies of corruption; the second section

discusses the theoretical underpinning of anti-

corruption strategy. The third part examines

selected cases of corruption while the fourth part

explores the various anti-corruption strategies

put in place by selected African States (Kenya

and Nigeria will be examined in details). The

next section highlights on the challenges and

prospects of anti-corruption in the continent. The

final section offers recommendations and

concludes the paper.

Clarification of Concepts

Theoretical and Thematic Foundation, Forms and

Typologies of Corruption

Corruption has no uniform definition. This is

because what is regarded as corruption depends

on the actors, the profiteers, initiators, how and

where it takes place. It also depends on the

existing laws and regulations guiding certain

actions. Some countries define corruption in the

broadest form while others legislated on the

narrow definition. The socio-cultural contests

and the time dimensions also make a unique

definition difficult. There are also levels of

corrupt practices. As a result of the fluidity and

the evolving nature of the term, the United

Nations (2000), the World Bank (1997),

Transparency International (1995), Khan(1996)

and ICPC Act (2000) among others have

adopted a descriptive approach and

criminalization of the act to describe what act is

corrupt. For example, the United Nations clearly

highlighted bribery, embezzlement, illicit

enrichment, abuse of office, laundering of

proceed of corruption, and obstruction of justice

among others as corrupt acts.

The World Bank (1997:2) defines corruption

as “the abuse of public power for private

benefit”. The Transparency International

(1995:1) defines it as “the abuse of entrusted

Manag. Stud. Econ. Syst., 3 (4), 225-243, Spring 2017

227

power for private gain,” Khan (1996:68) on the

other hand views corruption as the “behavior

that deviates from the formal rules of conduct

governing the action of someone in position of

public authority because of private motives such

as wealth, power or status”.

From the above theses corruption may be

divided into three types: extortive, manipulative

and nepotistic. The former refers to a situation

where one is forced to bribe in order to gain or

protect one’s rights or needs. The second refers

to an attempt to influence decisions in one’s

favor in any area of life. The last refers to

preferential treatment of relatives and friends in

appointments to positions, which can also

include organizational nepotism that is, special

favors given to political parties or organizations

(Eme et.al,2009).

For our purpose, corruption refers to any

behavior that deviates from the formal rules of

conduct governing the action of someone in

position of public trust and authority because of

private motives such as wealth, power or status.

This definition is significant because it identifies

corrupt acts to include fraud, bribery or other

improper actions or transactions aimed at

changing the course of events, judgments and

positions of trust. The activities of African

leader capture this descriptive definition of

corruption.

On the basis of the above definitions, the

basic characteristics of corruption are as follows:

1 It is a deliberate or intentional

exploitation of one’s position, status or resources;

2 It may be done directly or indirectly;

3 It is done for personal aggrandizement,

whether it is a material gain or an enhancement

of power, or prestige or influence;

4 It is done by violating legitimate or

sanctioned or commonly accepted norms of

behavior; and

5 It is done against the interest of the

community or other persons (Sharma and

Sadana, 2005:770).

Forms and Typologies of Kleptocratic States

According to Ackerman(1998), official

corruption can assume many forms depending

on how the paraphernalia of government is

organized or disorganized (Nwoye, 2000:102).

In her view, four types of Kleptocratic states can

be discerned:

1) Pure Kleptrocratic states

2) Bilateral monopoly states

3) Mafia – dominated states and

4) Competitive bribery states (Ackerman,

1998:36)

In Pure Kleptocratic States, the state

structure, the Head of government deliberately

organizes the political and economic system in

such a way to enhance his chances of extracting

rents and also reallocates these rents for personal

use (Ackerman, 1998:37). Most pure kleptocrats

often assume the role of “stationary bandit” as

long as their power remains unchallenged and

economically secure (Nwoye, 2000:102). For

instance Late president Mobutu Sese Seko of

Zaire (Congo Democratic), Nigeria under late

General Abacha and Gen.Olusegun Obasanjo,

and Idi Amin of Uganda can rightly be described

as pure kleptocrats. This is because the

fundamental concern of these political leaders is

primarily how to pillage, organize and

disorganize their states and economies to their

own selfish advantage, regardless of its effects to

ordinary populace. Abacha was discovered to

have stolen over $3.0 billion which was found in

his foreign accounts, apart from his investments

in physical assets (Ogunlana, 2007:11).

Not surprisingly, most pure kleptocratic

states are also highly repressive, and

authoritarian. There is scant regard for

democratic participation, rule of law, public

opinion and human rights. Under this climate of

fear and intimidation, the resources of the state

can easily be cornered in league with few

cronies who may see nothing wrong in the

arrangement. According to the EFCC and the

ICPC as at June, 2007, recovered about N613

billion involving 225 convictions (This Day,

March. 11, 2008). This represented about four

(4) percent of Federal and State budgetary

provisions for the period 2002 – 2006.

This was the tip of the iceberg in view of the

fact that the bulk of the fraud and corrupt

enrichment could not have been discovered.

Indeed, it has been estimated that up to 40

percent of government budget at all level was

lost to corrupt practices of government officials

at various stages.

In Bilateral monopoly states, the corrupt

ruler faces a single major briber to the extent that

the rent extractions are shared by the briber and

the ruler (Ackerman, 1998:44). The relative

228

strength of the two parties will obviously

determine how gains are shared as well as the

overall size of the benefits.

Ackerman (1998) goes on to posit that in

some bilateral monopoly states, the government

may even go into some form of alliance with a

mafia. A mafia can be regarded as an organized

crime group that provides protective and other

services that in ordinary societies are normally

provided by the state or its agencies. If some

rents can be generated only with the help of the

leader but the leader fears losing all the gains to

the briber, the chances are that the ruler will not

act.

Where a state depends on a few firms to

extract minerals or produce agricultural goods, it

is more likely that such firms may forge an

alliance with the country’s rulers to share the

wealth. Moreover, if the firm has invested

heavily in fixed capital or of its products is a

valuable raw material available only a few

places, the country’s leadership are in a

favorable position to extort more illegal rent

(Ackerman, 1998:44).

What worries me more than anything among

our problems, said former Nigerian President

Shehu Shagari in 1982, “is that of moral

decadence in our country, there is the problem of

bribery, corruption, lack of dedication to duty,

dishonesty, and all such vices” (Klitgaard,

1988:1).

He was right to worry. About a year later, his

civilian government was toppled in a military

coup, which the generals justified by the need to

control corruption. This topic dominated the new

regime’s policies, as foretold in its first press

conference in early 1984: “it is necessary to

reiterate that this new administration will not

tolerate fraud, corruption, squandermania, abuse

of public office for self or group, or other such

vices that characterized the administration of the

past four years (Klitgaard, 1988:1).

We have defined corruption both with

reference to the main actor involved, namely

persons at the highest levels of the political

system, and the purpose of the corrupt behavior,

namely to sustain the hold on power. Hence,

corruption can be for private and group

enrichment, and for power preservation

purposes. Often these forms of corruption are

linked. Corruption in the form of accumulation

or extraction occurs when government officials

use and abuse their hold on power to extract

from the private sector, from government

revenues, and from the economy at large. These

processes of accumulation have been called

extraction, rent-seeking, plunder, and

Kleptocracy (“rule by thieves”), depending on

the extent and context. Extraction takes place

mainly in the form of soliciting bribes in

procurement and government projects, in

privatization processes and in taxation. Military

procurement is known to be particularly affected

by extractive corruption worldwide, because of

the involvement of top\-level politicians, national

interest and secrecy. The cases below will

illustrate this thesis.

One example is the South African arms deal

scam, in which the then deputy president (now)

President Jacob Zuma allegedly solicited bribes

from an arms company in return for protecting

the company from investigation and giving it his

“permanent support”.

Another example is the military-political

corruption in Uganda. Here, the Tri-Star

Company obtained unusually generous favors

from the government (like start-up capital, tax

holidays, among others). This led some

parliamentarians to suggest that Kanathan, the

former owner of the company was a mere front

for President Yoweri Museveni. Another

example is Zimwe Construction Company

Limited, which has become one of the most

successful bidders for government construction

work. The company is successful because its

owners have significant connections with

technocrats and political ties with high-level

politicians (including the president).

Related to the above is the military-political

corruption in Uganda. Here army officers, senior

defense ministry officials and civilian

politicians, including President Museveni, have

benefited from Ugandan military operations in

neighboring countries. For instance, Ugandan

forces have advanced into areas of eastern

Congo to profit financially from the plunder of

natural resources. Congo has proven to be a

veritable treasure trove for a small number of

high ranking army officers who together with

their civilian counterparts have become rich

from this plunder.

From Kenya come the Golden berg and the

graft of the Kibaki regime. The Goldenberg

affairs was a gold and diamond re-export plan, in

229

which the government of former president Moi

paid the Goldenberg Company export subsidies

for exports that later proved fictitious. Witnesses

have given details of how former government

officials allegedly took part in looting

government resources through this fake gold and

jewellery export compensation scheme. But the

graft of the current Kibaki regime is also

evident, according to a report by the former

leader of the Kenyan Anti-corruption

Commission, John Githongo (see Business

Africa, 1998:35-38). Allegedly, senior officials

Theoretical Perspectives

This study will combine the pluralist and

social empowerment perspectives to the study of

anti-corruption strategies. There are various

ranges of approaches drawing from various

disciplines to the understanding of anti-

corruption strategies. Approaches to anti-

corruption grounded in public choice theory

emphasize economic reforms and downsizing/

rightsizing the state as the principal route to

reform, whereas the political economy approach

advocates conscious political intervention as the

fundamental vehicle for anti-corruption efforts.

The pluralist approach, in contrast assumes

that political initiatives centered on the creation

of new democratic institutions – such as elected

parliamentary committees and watch dog bodies

– are central to the success of efforts to control

corruption. Political reforms are thought to

contribute towards an environment which is

more conducive to reduced corruption because

they can increase the responsiveness of political

elites to the will of the people (Little, 1996).

Anti-corruption efforts centered on

institutional reforms are premised on a multi-

pronged approach which combines reforms in

the legal spheres (such as enforceable property

and contract rights and measures to enhance the

credibility of the judiciary), innovations in the

governance sphere (strengthening mechanisms

of accountability, controls over discretion and

resource use and improvements in terms and

conditions of employments for civil servants)

and specific institutional mechanisms (such as

creating an anti-corruption agency, special

courts to review corruption cases, and asset

declaration for politicians and civil servants)

(Robinson, 1998).

This approach may be appropriate and

effective in countries where corruption is not

entrenched and where anti-corruption laws,

agencies and organizations are in place and have

public support. Such societies invariably tend to

have the institutional trappings of democracy

with governments that are subject to electoral

contestation and popular accountability. But

while political competition offers opportunities

for new political elites to gain legitimacy by

taking action against corruption, it can also

enable such elites to secure greater access to

existing rent-seeking opportunities as evidence

from Africa appears to indicate. However,

approaches rooted in these traditions tend to

confine analysis to particular countries and

institutions and frequently overlook the role

international actors in shaping the form and

content of corrupt practices at the national level.

The creation of democratic institutions and

special agencies to combat corruption will only

succeed if citizens organize themselves

effectively. In this respect Riley (1997) advances

the notion of “social empowerment”, which he

uses to refer to the range of political and

economic resources and alternatives available to

citizens, as an integral element of an assault on

entrenched or systemic corruption. Actions by

organized citizens on complement institutional

reforms and provide them with a proper social

foundation which is indispensable to their success.

Spontaneous public demonstrations against

corrupt politicians have been effective in

prompting authorities to remove them from

office in some polities (the dismissals of the

governments of late Benazir Bhutto in Pakistan,

Color de Melloin Brazil, Shurhato and

Thaistinawat in Indonesia) and the recent clamor

for the arrest and retrial of James Ibori,

Babangida among others are examples but they

do not take tackle the root causes of the problem

when it permeates all levels of government

machinery. At best such actions can lead to a

temporary abatement of the problem but it soon

resurfaces in other guises. Today, “social

empowerment” framework has been

strengthened by the activities of the organized

civil society organizations such as Transparency

in Nigeria (TIN); Coalition Against Corruption

(CACOL); publish what you pay Nigeria

(PWYPN) among others. But while some

organizations with civil society can be a potent

force for anti-corruption efforts, other groups

benefit from corruption and are resistant to

change. This suggests that independent actions

by Independent Civil Groups have its

limitations, the needs to be complimented by

institutional interventions.

Africa and Anti-Corruption Strategies

Serious attempts to control corruption are

often as old as corruption itself (Riley,

1998:132). A recent study by Sen (1997) and

Noon (1984) point to some early examples. In

ancient China, many public officials were paid a

corruption-preventing allowance to try to ensure

their continued honesty. This illustration relates

to recent debates about the linkage between the

low salary levels of junior civil servants and

levels of corruption in the continent. Kautilya, a

fourth century BC Indian political analyst,

sought to identify forty different ways in which

public officials could be corrupt. He also

developed a system of spot-checks to reduce

corruption, which were accompanied by a

rewards and penalties system. Such ancient

examples of attempted corruption-control are

similar to those developed by public officials

and academic analysts in recent years, in the

period since the 1960s (Riley, 1998:132).

Broadly speaking, there are four levels or types

of anti-corruption strategies which can be

identified in operation in most post-

independence Africa: International, national,

local; and populist (Theobald, 1990).

Since the mid-1990s a series of international

anti-corruption initiatives has emerged (OECD,

1997; Kaufmann, 1997; Rose-Ackerman, 1997\],

but earlier decades saw African countries

themselves develop strategies based upon

national and local action including anti-

corruption agencies, public inquiries, inspector-

general systems, legal and quasi-legal trials,

complaints procedures, and public awareness

campaigns \[Clarke, 1983; Doig, 1995;

Heidenheimer, LeVine and Johnston, 1989;

IRIS, 1996\]. Often a key issue in assessing the

effectiveness and sustainability of such strategies

is the commitment of the powerful to act

effectively to curb corruption (Klitgaard, 1997;

Kpundeh, 1997). Populist initiatives such as

purges of civil servants and former politicians

have not had much success, although the issue of

corruption has acquired great political salience

in recent years due to the actions of NGOs and

activism by lawyers and other public interest

More recently, several countries have

adopted public integrity reforms which are

associated with the ‘New Public Management’

approach to governance in western societies.

These initiatives are often linked to the influence

of aid donors or the activities of pressure groups

such as Transparency International (TI).

Examples include new administrative procedures

such as overlapping jurisdictions (where two or

more officials are responsible for an

administrative action), service delivery surveys

(for example in Tanzania and Uganda, in

cooperation with the World Bank), and structural

reform, where an administrative machine is

decentralized or deregulation takes place.

However, there are several potential problems

with such strategies. For example,

decentralization, a widely touted remedy for

many of the African state’s contemporary ills,

can also create lower-level corruption unless it is

accompanied by some of the range of possible

anti-corruption strategies. Nevertheless, aid

donors and others hope that these reforms will

improve public integrity either directly or

indirectly.

Many of the less coercive anti-corruption

efforts are based upon the manipulation of

incentives for, and the potential punishments to

be meted out to, public officials. These modern

strategies are often accompanied by attempts to

improve both recruitment of public officials who

are more likely to be honest and better

information upon their preferably honest public

studies (Gould, 1980; McKinney and Johnston,

1986; Klitgaard, 1988). The anti-corruption

strategy proposed is usually based upon a

distinctive view of the causes and character of

corruption and anti-corruption strategies:

economic analyses; mass public opinion

perspectives; and institutional viewpoints.

Developed since the 1960s, these are outlined

and evaluated in a wide variety of publications

(Heidenheimer, LeVine and Johnston, 1989).

Economic analyses prioritize the principal-agent

market relationship to identify corruption and

anti-corruption strategies, whereas mass public

opinion perspectives examine the social or

cultural context of corruption and suggest as a

result mass attitudinal change or civic awareness

anti-corruption strategies. These two approaches

are well established and well regarded, with an

extensive academic literature and some policy

applications. A third and newer, institutional

approach focuses upon the public sector and

institutional reform (Doig, 1995; Stapenhurst

and Langseth, 1997). This is important because

it enables the analyst of corruption to suggest

short-term and specific policy recommendations

which focus upon, low-level corruption. This

newer approach has yet to have a major impact

upon policy formation. The table below

Anti-Corruption in Uganda

Corruption is actually a serious crime that

can undermine the social and economic

development of society. Transparency

International, a UK based anti-corruption

watchdog defines corruption as the abuse of

entrusted power for dishonest gain. No country

is immune to corruption, but some countries are

more corrupt than others. Uganda is currently

viewed as one of the most corrupt countries in

the world despite reported improvement in the

country’s corruption ranking.

Recent studies have given strong indications

that corruption in Uganda is endemic and yet the

government has put in place one of the most

comprehensive anti-corruption measures in

Africa. Institutions established to fight

corruption include the Inspectorate of

Government, Directorate of Ethics & Integrity,

Anti Corruption court, and Public Procurement

& Disposal of Public Assets Authority. A legal

framework that allows these institutions to

operate effectively is also in place and this

includes the Leadership Code and the Prevention

of Corruption Act.

More so, civil society organizations have

Some people attribute it to lack of political will

misappropriation of CHOGM funds and Global

have been handled. For instance the DP leader,
